```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/tema.R")
```

## The problem {#sec-problem}

When exercise stops, heart rate does not drop at once: it descends towards
rest along a roughly exponential curve. The early part of that descent
mostly reflects vagal reactivation [@imai1994], and a slow recovery over the
first minute is associated with higher mortality [@cole1999]. The speed of
recovery is therefore a cheap, non-invasive window onto the autonomic
control of the heart.

The simplest model that captures the idea is

$$
\mathrm{HR}(t) \;=\; \mathrm{HR}_\infty + A\,e^{-t/\tau} + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),
$$ {#eq-model}

where $\mathrm{HR}_\infty$ is the resting rate, $A$ the amplitude of the
descent and $\tau$ the **time constant**: the number of seconds heart rate
takes to cover 63% of the way back. We want to estimate $\tau$ and, above
all, to know *how much* we know about it.

## Data with a known truth {#sec-data}

To be able to check the method we simulate a five-minute recovery, sampled
every five seconds, with parameters we know.

```{r}
#| label: fig-data
#| fig-cap: "Simulated recovery: observations (points) and true curve (dashed line)."
set.seed(1930)

hr_mean <- function(t, hr_rest, A, tau) hr_rest + A * exp(-t / tau)

truth <- c(hr_rest = 68, A = 62, tau = 75, sigma = 3)
t <- seq(0, 300, by = 5)
y <- hr_mean(t, 68, 62, 75) + rnorm(length(t), 0, truth[["sigma"]])
dat <- data.frame(t, y)

ggplot(dat, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_function(fun = hr_mean, args = list(hr_rest = 68, A = 62, tau = 75),
                linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey45") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Time since end of exercise (s)", y = "Heart rate (bpm)")
```

## The Bayesian model {#sec-bayes}

Three of the four parameters are positive. Rather than imposing
constraints, we work on an unconstrained scale,

$$
\boldsymbol{\phi} = \bigl(\mathrm{HR}_\infty,\; \log A,\; \log\tau,\; \log\sigma\bigr),
$$

and place the priors directly on $\boldsymbol{\phi}$:

| Parameter | Prior | 95% prior interval |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $\mathrm{HR}_\infty$ | $\mathcal{N}(70,\,15^2)$ | 41 to 99 bpm |
| $\log A$ | $\mathcal{N}(\log 60,\,0.5^2)$ | $A$ between 23 and 160 bpm |
| $\log\tau$ | $\mathcal{N}(\log 60,\,0.75^2)$ | $\tau$ between 14 and 261 s |
| $\log\sigma$ | $\mathcal{N}(\log 3,\,1^2)$ | $\sigma$ between 0.4 and 21 bpm |

: Weakly informative priors. {#tbl-priors}

These priors rule out the physiologically absurd and little else. By Bayes'
theorem, the posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior,

$$
p(\boldsymbol{\phi} \mid y) \;\propto\;
\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(y_i \mid \mathrm{HR}_\infty + A\,e^{-t_i/\tau},\, \sigma^2\bigr)
\; p(\boldsymbol{\phi}),
$$ {#eq-posterior}

and in R all we need is its logarithm:

```{r}
#| label: log-posterior
log_posterior <- function(phi, t, y) {
  mu <- phi[1] + exp(phi[2]) * exp(-t / exp(phi[3]))
  sum(dnorm(y, mu, exp(phi[4]), log = TRUE)) +   # likelihood
    dnorm(phi[1], 70, 15, log = TRUE) +           # priors
    dnorm(phi[2], log(60), 0.5, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(phi[3], log(60), 0.75, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(phi[4], log(3), 1, log = TRUE)
}
```

## Metropolis in twenty lines {#sec-metropolis}

The normalising constant of @eq-posterior is a four-dimensional integral
that we never need to compute. The Metropolis algorithm
[@metropolis1953; @hastings1970] builds a Markov chain whose stationary
distribution is the posterior using only *ratios* of densities, in which
that constant cancels.

::: {#def-metropolis}
## Random-walk Metropolis

Given the current state $\boldsymbol{\phi}$:

1. propose $\boldsymbol{\phi}' = \boldsymbol{\phi} + \boldsymbol{\eta}$, with
   $\boldsymbol{\eta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s}^2))$;
2. accept the proposal with probability
   $\alpha = \min\!\bigl\{1,\; p(\boldsymbol{\phi}' \mid y) \,/\, p(\boldsymbol{\phi} \mid y)\bigr\}$;
3. if rejected, repeat $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ as the next state.
:::

```{r}
#| label: metropolis
metropolis <- function(log_post, init, n_iter, step, ...) {
  d <- length(init)
  chain <- matrix(NA_real_, n_iter, d)
  current <- init
  lp <- log_post(current, ...)
  accepted <- 0L
  for (i in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    proposal <- current + rnorm(d, 0, step)
    lp_prop <- log_post(proposal, ...)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_prop - lp) {          # accept with probability α
      current <- proposal
      lp <- lp_prop
      accepted <- accepted + 1L
    }
    chain[i, ] <- current
  }
  list(chain = chain, acceptance = accepted / n_iter)
}
```

We launch four chains from dispersed starting points. The step sizes in
`step` were tuned by hand until the acceptance rate fell within the range
regarded as efficient: between 0.23, the theoretical optimum in high
dimension [@roberts1997], and 0.44, the optimum for a single parameter.

```{r}
#| label: sampling
n_iter <- 30000
step <- c(0.45, 0.02, 0.04, 0.09)

chains <- lapply(1:4, function(k) {
  init <- c(rnorm(1, 70, 10), log(60) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.4),
            log(60) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.6), log(3) + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5))
  metropolis(log_posterior, init, n_iter, step, t = t, y = y)
})

round(sapply(chains, `[[`, "acceptance"), 3)
```

## Did it converge? {#sec-diagnostics}

Before looking at results, the chains deserve some distrust.
@fig-traces shows the first iterations of $\tau$: all four forget their
starting point within a few hundred steps and then mix together.

```{r}
#| label: fig-traces
#| fig-cap: "Trace plots of $\\tau$ over the first 3000 iterations of the four chains (one shade of grey per chain). After a short transient they explore the same region."
#| fig-height: 3.3
traces <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(k) {
  data.frame(iter = 1:3000, tau = exp(chains[[k]]$chain[1:3000, 3]),
             chain = factor(k))
}))

ggplot(traces, aes(iter, tau, colour = chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dd_tinta, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = expression(tau ~ "(s, log scale)"))
```

We discard the first half of each chain as warm-up and compute the
$\widehat{R}$ statistic [@gelman2013], which compares between-chain and
within-chain variance; values close to 1 indicate that all chains describe
the same distribution.

```{r}
#| label: rhat
posterior <- lapply(chains, function(x) x$chain[(n_iter / 2 + 1):n_iter, ])

rhat <- function(lst, j) {
  m <- sapply(lst, function(x) x[, j])
  n <- nrow(m)
  B <- n * var(colMeans(m))            # between-chain variance
  W <- mean(apply(m, 2, var))          # within-chain variance
  sqrt(((n - 1) / n * W + B / n) / W)
}

setNames(round(sapply(1:4, rhat, lst = posterior), 3),
         c("hr_rest", "log_A", "log_tau", "log_sigma"))
```

## What we learned {#sec-results}

We pool the four chains and return to the natural scale.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-posterior
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior summary against the values used to simulate the data."
phi <- do.call(rbind, posterior)
draws <- data.frame(hr_rest = phi[, 1], A = exp(phi[, 2]),
                    tau = exp(phi[, 3]), sigma = exp(phi[, 4]))

tab <- t(sapply(draws, resumen_posterior))
tab <- cbind(truth = truth[rownames(tab)], tab)
rownames(tab) <- c("$\\mathrm{HR}_\\infty$ (bpm)", "$A$ (bpm)",
                   "$\\tau$ (s)", "$\\sigma$ (bpm)")

knitr::kable(tab, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Truth", "Mean", "SD", "2.5%", "97.5%"))
```

```{r}
#| label: numbers
#| include: false
ci_tau <- quantile(draws$tau, c(0.025, 0.975))
hrr60 <- draws$A * (1 - exp(-60 / draws$tau))
ci_hrr <- quantile(hrr60, c(0.025, 0.975))
rho <- cor(phi[, 1], phi[, 3])
fmt <- function(x, d = 1) format(round(x, d), nsmall = d)
```

The posterior mean of $\tau$ is `r fmt(mean(draws$tau))` s, with a 95%
credible interval from `r fmt(ci_tau[1])` to `r fmt(ci_tau[2])` s, which
contains the true value of 75 s. @fig-tau shows the whole Bayesian update:
a prior that allowed anything from 14 to 261 s ends up, after 61
observations, concentrated in a range of about `r round(diff(ci_tau))`
seconds.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tau
#| fig-cap: "Prior (dashed) and posterior (solid) of the time constant $\\tau$. The dotted vertical line marks the true value."
#| fig-height: 3.5
grid <- data.frame(tau = seq(20, 160, length.out = 400))
grid$prior <- dlnorm(grid$tau, log(60), 0.75)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(tau, prior, linetype = "Prior"), grid, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_density(aes(tau, linetype = "Posterior"), draws, fill = "grey60",
               alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.55, key_glyph = "path") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 75, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = "dashed", Posterior = "solid")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20, 160)) +
  labs(x = expression(tau ~ "(s)"), y = "Density")
```

A more demanding check is the **posterior predictive**: simulate new data
from the fitted model and see whether they look like the observed ones.

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictive
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check. Dark band: 95% interval for the mean curve. Light band: 95% interval for new observations. Points: data."
sub <- draws[sample(nrow(draws), 2000), ]
tg <- seq(0, 300, by = 2)

curves <- sapply(tg, function(s) hr_mean(s, sub$hr_rest, sub$A, sub$tau))
new_y <- curves + rnorm(length(curves), 0, sub$sigma)

band <- function(m) apply(m, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
pred <- data.frame(t = tg, mean = colMeans(curves),
                   c_lo = band(curves)[1, ], c_hi = band(curves)[2, ],
                   y_lo = band(new_y)[1, ], y_hi = band(new_y)[2, ])

ggplot(pred, aes(t)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = y_lo, ymax = y_hi), fill = "grey50", alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = c_lo, ymax = c_hi), fill = "grey20", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean)) +
  geom_point(aes(t, y), dat, size = 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Time since end of exercise (s)", y = "Heart rate (bpm)")
```

## From parameters to the clinical index {#sec-derived}

The practical advantage of having posterior *draws* is that the uncertainty
of any derived quantity comes for free. The usual clinical index is
heart rate recovery at one minute,

$$
\mathrm{HRR}_{60} \;=\; \mathrm{HR}(0) - \mathrm{HR}(60) \;=\; A\,\bigl(1 - e^{-60/\tau}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-hrr}

and its posterior distribution is obtained by applying @eq-hrr to every
draw:

```{r}
#| label: hrr60
hrr60 <- draws$A * (1 - exp(-60 / draws$tau))
round(resumen_posterior(hrr60), 1)
```

That is, `r fmt(mean(hrr60))` bpm, with a 95% interval from
`r fmt(ci_hrr[1])` to `r fmt(ci_hrr[2])` bpm (the true value is
`r fmt(62 * (1 - exp(-60 / 75)))`). No delta method or asymptotic
approximation was needed.

## Limits and what comes next {#sec-limits}

Two honest caveats. The first is statistical: $\mathrm{HR}_\infty$ and
$\log\tau$ are strongly correlated in the posterior ($\rho =$
`r fmt(rho, 2)`), because a slower recovery towards a lower resting rate
looks very much like a faster one towards a higher resting rate. A random
walk with independent steps explores such diagonal ridges poorly; that is
why a four-parameter problem needed tens of thousands of iterations.
Hamiltonian methods handle this far better.

The second is physiological: @eq-model assumes independent errors, but real
heart rate fluctuates with memory. Neighbouring beats resemble each other.
Ignoring this makes the intervals too optimistic. The remedy is to model
the noise as a stochastic process with temporal correlation, and the
simplest of them all is the
[Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process](../ornstein-uhlenbeck/index.qmd).
